title: Merlin's Cave: How a Queen Used Magic to Sell Her Dynasty
summary: In 1735, Queen Caroline of Brandenburg-Ansbach did something that left her courtiers scratching their heads. She commissioned a mysterious grotto in the gardens of her palace at Richmond, filled with wax figures of Merlin, King Arthur, and other legendary figures from Britain's mythic past. Contemporaries dismissed it as "a great many strange puppets," but Caroline was playing a long game. She was the wife of King George II, a German prince from the House of Hanover who had inherited the British throne just two decades earlier. Many Britons still viewed the Hanoverians as foreign interlopers, and the king's public feud with his son, Frederick, Prince of Wales, threatened to destabilize the monarchy. Caroline's solution was to tap into the power of Arthurian legend. Unlike the Jacobites, who claimed the throne through hereditary right, Arthur and Merlin belonged to no single dynasty. By associating her family with these iconic figures, Caroline aimed to forge a new kind of legitimacy—one rooted in patriotism and a shared British identity. Merlin, in particular, was a clever choice. In Arthurian tradition, he is an adviser and prophet who guides the king and foretells the realm's destiny. By placing Merlin at the center of her cave, Caroline linked the Hanoverians to Britain's ancient heritage and its future success. The symbolism was not lost on her contemporaries. A 1735 poem by Jane Brereton had Merlin urge Frederick to fulfill his filial duty and "perpetuate Brunswick's race," suggesting the cave was a plea for family harmony. But not everyone was convinced. Satirists like Nicholas Amhurst, writing under the pseudonym Caleb D'Anvers, mocked the cave as an eccentric folly. Opposition writers used Merlin as a vehicle to attack Caroline and her ally, Robert Walpole, Britain's first de facto prime minister. Scholar Amanda S. Meixell notes that Merlin became "an object of ridicule, closely associated with the minister, the devilish 'wizard' who could not be trusted." Yet the very fact that critics parodied the cave shows they understood its political message. They disagreed with it, but they couldn't ignore it. Merlin's Cave offers a fascinating glimpse into the political uses of myth. Caroline understood that legitimacy isn't just about birth—it's about the stories a nation tells about itself. And sometimes, a magic cave is just what you need to rewrite the narrative.
why_it_matters: The story reveals how political power is often built on stories and symbols, not just bloodlines — and it shows that arguing over who controls a nation's history is something people have done for centuries.

background_read: Merlin's Cave was a real garden building built in 1735 at Richmond, the palace of Queen Caroline of Brandenburg-Ansbach, the German-born wife of King George II.

George II came from the House of Hanover, a German family that had taken the British throne only two decades earlier, and many Britons still thought of them as foreign interlopers; supporters of the exiled Stuart dynasty, known as Jacobites, wanted to restore the old royal line by hereditary right.

Caroline hoped that filling a cave with wax figures of Merlin, King Arthur, and other legendary characters would connect her family to Britain's ancient past, because Arthur and Merlin belonged to no particular dynasty and could therefore stand for a shared British patriotism rather than a blood claim.

Opposition writers such as Nicholas Amhurst mocked the cave and used Merlin to attack Caroline's chief minister, Robert Walpole, who acted as Britain's first prime minister in all but name; later historians like Amanda S. Meixell argue that the critics' mockery proved how clearly everyone understood the cave as political symbolism.
The episode shows how 'Merlin's Cave' became a shorthand for the idea that a nation's history can be purposefully used to make a new ruling family feel ancient and legitimate.

perspectives.description: Caroline used creativity and intelligence to strengthen her family's position. By connecting the Hanoverians to beloved British legends, she built a more inclusive, patriotic source of loyalty.
Opposition writers saw the grotto as propaganda: wasteful, absurd, and designed to hide a foreign dynasty's weak claim. Their satires treated Merlin as a symbol of manipulation.
The cave is a case study in political myth-making: both supporters and critics understood that symbols carry meaning, and each side worked to define that meaning for the public.

Merlin's Cave prefigures modern debates about statues, flags, and national storytelling. It reminds us that people in power will keep using history to justify their authority, so citizens need to question those stories.
